title: SQL Alone Isn’t Enough: Why Modern Applications Need More Than Just SQL
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
The long-standing debate between SQL and NoSQL used to be framed as a choice between structured and unstructured data. However, this distinction has become less clear. SQL databases can now store unstructured data, such as binary JSON, while NoSQL can be designed with entities structured in collections, whether referenced or embedded.

Despite the increasing popularity of SQL databases, developers today rarely rely on raw SQL and JDBC alone. Instead, they are utilizing NoSQL-like APIs to simplify mapping application objects to databases. Object-relational mappers (ORMs), GraphQL, and REST APIs (like ORDS and PostgREST) have been used to avoid native SQL queries. Other solutions include MongoDB-compatible APIs, such as the Oracle Database API for MongoDB, FerretDB, or Pongo, alongside other document-based models like Oracle's SODA and JSON-Relational Duality Views.

Even a fan of SQL like me recognizes that application developers rarely want to work directly in SQL.

YugabyteDB's compatibility with PostgreSQL is a strategic choice because it capitalizes on PostgreSQL's extensive ecosystem of tools, frameworks, proxies, and ORMs, which are widely used in all applications. YugabyteDB also stores rows as documents at the storage level to get more flexibility compared to traditional databases and their 8k block size.

Developers often work with documents stored in document databases or converged relational databases that support document capabilities. Instead of directly using JDBC to pass SQL queries and retrieve a single result set, they typically utilize libraries that provide an Application Programming Interface (API) that aligns more closely with their coding languages. While this approach feels natural for many developers, it can create challenges for some database administrators who consider SQL the sole method for managing persistent data.

What's wrong with SQL as an API?

I've always been enthusiastic about relational databases and SQL. Still, I recognize an inherent paradox: relational structures exist only within the database, and SQL alone cannot fully connect these structures with the application.

The beauty of the relational model lies in its simplicity. Complex data is organized into loosely coupled, two-dimensional tables. For instance, consider a table of employees and a separate table of departments modeled as distinct entities. Departments can exist, be queried, and managed independently of employees, and vice versa. This loose coupling is achieved through foreign keys, which link entities by logical addresses rather than physical pointers. This approach offers many advantages, such as data independence, evolutivity, and avoiding update anomalies.

With SQL, you can manipulate these tables as independent sets, allowing for operations like INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE for each table individually. Within an ACID transaction, these operations ensure a consistent state and help prevent anomalies. This works well as a command language, especially with interactive graphical user interface (GUI) or command line (CLI) interfaces.

Yet, SQL presents some limitations as an application programming interface (API). Applications do not typically use data in the form of simple relational tables. Instead, they often work with object graphs or nested structures called documents. For example, a Department object in code might contain a list of Employee objects. Whether the application treats it as a single document or not, storing or retrieving such hierarchical objects in a relational database necessitates multiple SQL statements for each table or complex join queries that flatten the structure into a single two-dimensional result set, resulting in redundancy for many-to-one relationships. Thus, while SQL is designed for relational databases, it undermines the advantages of relational structures when interacting with applications and cannot even return a hierarchical structure.

I'll illustrate this with two slides from a presentation I gave at POUG to help DBAs understand the need for ORMs like Hibernate.

📤 SELECT output API is one single flattened table

When you SELECT to get rows from multiple entities to form your application document, you will either run one query per entity, resulting in inefficient roundtrips (and inconsistencies if using Read Committed isolation level), or a single query with join, and resulting in redundant column values:


Advanced ORMs let you choose the fetching type and method to get the best performance depending on your database and use cases. You must use an Object-Relational Mapping framework to de-duplicate this result into multiple objects:

📥 INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE input API is an array of scalar values

It's the same when writing to the database. SQL cannot take an object graph or a whole document as an input. You have to execute multiple DML statements, one per table, and those statements do not even take a table-like structure but a list of scalar values.

The question marks in the SQL text here represent placeholders for scalar values, and it is not uncommon to find INSERT statements like this: 

INSERT INTO departments VALUES (
  (?,?,?,?) 
);
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (
  (?,?,?,?,?,?) ,
  (?,?,?,?,?,?) ,
  (?,?,?,?,?,?) 
);

This is not a practical API to send data to the database, mainly when data is already structured in objects or documents in the application. Except for bulk-loading from CSV files, application developers want to send one document and get the database to update its relational structures.

How did we get a non-relational input/output API for SQL?

Understanding SQL’s role as a command language—not as an API—clarifies why it doesn’t meet today’s application needs directly. To understand why SQL was not developed as an API between applications and databases, we must consider the architecture of database applications when they first emerged. Back then, there was no clear separation of concerns between the application and the database, and object-oriented programming had not yet been used for database applications. Today's SQL databases are a small component of the original relational database management systems (RDBMS).

Data-centric applications running in RDBMS

SQL is a command language created for directly manipulating relational tables within a database rather than serving as an API between an application and a persistence layer. To illustrate this, I examined the user guide for the first commercial SQL database, Oracle 2.3, released in April 1981. This guide consists of eight books: 

- ORACLE SQL LANGUAGE USER'S GUIDE - 99 pages
- ORACLE SQL LANGUAGE REFERENCE GUIDE - 54 pages
- ORACLE TERMINAL INTERFACE USER FRIENDLY INTERFACE (UFI) - 15 pages
- ORACLE INTERACTIVE APPLICATION FACILITY USER'S GUIDE - 110 pages
- ORACLE REPORT WRITER/TEXT FORMATTER USER'S GUIDE - 104 pages
- ORACLE HOST LANGUAGE INTERFACE - 85 pages
- ORACLE DATABASE ADMINISTRATOR'S GUIDE - 41 pages
- ORACLE INSTALLATION GUIDE - 39 pages

From the beginning of Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMS), three interfaces connected the database to the users, using SQL as their language: command interface, application interface, and host language embedding. This setup differs from modern deployments, which primarily utilize only the SQL language component of the database, while the application front-end and back-end operate separately.

  • The User-Friendly Interface (UFI) was later renamed SQL*Plus and was used to run interactive SQL statements. Input data was text, and the result was displayed in a terminal as one table. A BREAK command was added to hide the redundant column values.
  • The Interactive Application Facility (IAF) was later renamed SQL*Forms. It defined the presentation view with blocks mapped to the SQL tables, and the trigger-based controller generated one statement per table. The transaction remained open between user interactions because the user had a single remote terminal (CRT). The code ran on the database server, so roundtrips were not a problem.
  • The Host Language Interface was for procedural language precompilers, later renamed Pro*Fortran, Pro*C, and Pro*COBOL. In those languages, the data structures are mapped to two-dimensional tables, like in the COBOL data division.

RDBMS were built as a platform to run applications and we retained mostly the SQL database part of it. I used the example of Oracle, but it was the same for INGRES which came with a full wysiwig application development environment.

Later, the SQL-92 standard also defined these classes of SQL statements:

The SQL standard considered applications such as in-database stored procedures (modules), preprocessed procedural language, interactive statements, and dynamic or prepared statements. SQL is ideally suited for this environment with text-based commands. These commands can be typed directly into a terminal, generated by an application runtime, or transformed into a database call interface (such as OCI) using precompilers. However, 20 years later, the software engineering landscape revolutionized, moving towards multi-tasking, client/server architectures, three-tier systems, and object-oriented programming languages. The "direct invocation" is used through client-server libraries like JDBC but requires a proper API to integrate with the application objects.

SQL In The Modern Application Stack

With modern application architectures moving towards microservices, serverless computing, and multi-tier systems, SQL’s role as a standalone command language no longer meets the needs of today’s applications. Attempts to evolve SQL and RDBMS, such as object-oriented DBMS, which stores objects rather than relations, and SQLJ, which pre-compiles Java, never became popular. The application architect had three solutions:

  • Data-centric applications often use stored procedures to encapsulate all business logic (see the idea of SmartDB) and, in some cases, include the presentation layer, as seen in Oracle APEX. While this approach suits small applications, it limits programming languages and creates vendor lock-in.

  • Use an Object-Relational Mapper to generate the SQL text from an Object-Oriented database API. This works but is complex to design efficiently, given the impedance mismatch between the application and the database structures.
  • Use a NoSQL document database, like DynamoDB or MongoDB, with a simple GET/PUT API to load/store the application objects in/out of the database. They provide client libraries that call the database like any web service rather than establishing stateful connections.

Besides, some applications interact with the relational database, like a NoSQL database, through an additional proxy or view. They can expose a REST API from the database (like ORDS or PostgREST). Some add a proxy to add an API compatible with a document database, like Oracle Database API for MongoDB or FerretDB. Oracle recently extended the SQL views to provide an updatable document-like view on relational tables. Those solutions are still vendor-specific, and there is no open standard for a document API. GraphQL was also popular a few years ago, offering an abstraction over databases, but the performance of the SQL generated may be problematic.

This article clarifies that a database application requires an API that extends beyond SQL. From a database perspective, this approach may appear less efficient than one that is database-centric. While there are many possible solutions, ranging from Object-Relational Mapping to Document Databases, the key considerations are not just the reliability of the database itself. When choosing a database and the API, it's also essential to consider the surrounding ecosystem and the job market to find developers skilled in the chosen technology stack.

In Conclusion

The debate between SQL and NoSQL has evolved beyond simply comparing structured and unstructured data. It now focuses on how applications interact with data using appropriate APIs. Modern applications require flexible and friendly access to their data, whether through Object-Relational Mappers (ORMs), GraphQL, REST APIs, or the protocols of document-based databases that inherently support hierarchical data structures.

The resurgence of SQL databases, like open-source PostgreSQL-compatible services such as YugabyteDB, provides developers with many tools, extensions, and compatibility with emerging technologies, giving them more choices than ever. On the other hand, NoSQL databases remain attractive due to their quick setup, minimal intermediate layers, and user-friendly data handling, which fits well with modern application developer experience. The compatibility of the APIs is critical to allowing developers freedom.

Ultimately, SQL databases are popular but combined with some NoSQL API to provide the best developer experience. The SQL languages evolve, but document-based APIs are provided on top of them for relational databases. By understanding the strengths and trade-offs of each option, organizations can select the right combination of tools to bridge the gap between database technology and application needs.
